entries.label: mott6-c-0001
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — design-factor
entries.text: mott6-c-0001 machine elements in mechanical design — design-factor mott defines the design factor n as a measure of the relative safety of a load-carrying component. in most cases the strength of the material is divided by n to obtain a design stress (also called the allowable stress), and the actual stress must be less than the design stress. design factor n is defined as a measure of the relative safety of a load-carrying component; the material strength divided by the design factor gives the design (allowable) stress

entries.label: mott6-c-0002
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — design-factor
entries.text: mott6-c-0002 machine elements in mechanical design — design-factor mott states that the value of the design factor or design stress is often governed by codes from standards-setting organizations, and that some companies adopt their own policies based on past experience. value of the design factor is governed by codes established by standards-setting organizations, or by company policy

entries.label: mott6-c-0003
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — design-factor
entries.text: mott6-c-0003 machine elements in mechanical design — design-factor mott states that in the absence of codes or standards the designer must use judgement to specify the desired design factor. selection of the design factor requires designer judgement when no code or standard applies

entries.label: mott6-c-0010
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — fatigue
entries.text: mott6-c-0010 machine elements in mechanical design — fatigue mott states that no specific dividing line can be defined between low-cycle and high-cycle fatigue, and that designers often use up to 1000 cycles for low-cycle fatigue and higher numbers, up to infinite life, for high-cycle fatigue. boundary between low-cycle and high-cycle fatigue is not sharply definable; designers often take up to about 1000 cycles as low-cycle fatigue

entries.label: mott6-c-0011
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — fatigue
entries.text: mott6-c-0011 machine elements in mechanical design — fatigue mott states that fatigue failures frequently occur within areas of stress concentration such as keyways or grooves in shafts, steps in the size of a cross section, notches and other geometric discontinuities, and that even surface roughness or accidental nicks can initiate cracks. fatigue failures frequently occur at areas of stress concentration such as keyways or grooves in shafts, steps in cross section, and notches

entries.label: mott6-c-0012
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — fatigue
entries.text: mott6-c-0012 machine elements in mechanical design — fatigue mott states that fatigue failures start at small surface cracks, internal imperfections, or grain boundaries in areas subjected to tensile stress, and grow with repeated stress application until the component fails, often suddenly. fatigue cracks initiate at small surface cracks, internal imperfections or grain boundaries in areas subjected to tensile stress

entries.label: mott6-c-0020
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0020 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that the square key is the most common type of key for shafts up to 6 1/2 in in diameter, and that the rectangular key is recommended for larger shafts and used for smaller shafts where the reduced height can be tolerated. square key is the most common key type for shafts up to 6.5 inches in diameter

entries.label: mott6-c-0021
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0021 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that for the preferred parallel key dimensions tabulated against shaft diameter, the key width is approximately one-quarter of the shaft diameter. parallel key width is approximately one quarter of the shaft diameter

entries.label: mott6-c-0022
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0022 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that radiused keyseats and chamfered keys can be used to reduce stress concentrations, and cites suggested values from ansi standard b17.1. radiused keyseats and chamfered keys reduce stress concentrations

entries.label: mott6-c-0023
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0023 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that the taper key design gives a smaller bearing area on the sides of the key and that the bearing stress must therefore be checked. taper key has a smaller bearing area on the sides of the key than a parallel key, so the bearing stress must be checked

entries.label: mott6-c-0024
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0024 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that lower stress concentration factors result from the pin key design as compared with parallel or taper keys, and that a close fit between pin and groove is required so that bearing is uniform along the pin. pin key produces lower stress concentration factors than parallel or taper keys

entries.label: mott6-c-0025
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0025 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that where light loading and relatively easy assembly and disassembly are desired, the woodruff key should be considered. woodruff key should be considered where loading is light and relatively easy assembly and disassembly are desired

entries.label: mott6-c-0026
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0026 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott recommends that low-carbon steel sae 1018 be considered for most key applications in this book's problem solutions, being low cost and readily available with generally adequate strength, and lists higher-strength and corrosion-resistant alternatives. key material is recommended to be low-carbon steel sae 1018 for most applications in this book's problems

entries.label: mott6-c-0040
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0040 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that splines perform the same function as a key in transmitting torque from the shaft to the mating element, a spline being a series of axial keys machined into the shaft with corresponding grooves in the bore of the mating part. splines perform the same function as a key in transmitting torque from shaft to mating element

entries.label: mott6-c-0041
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0041 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that the advantages of splines over keys are many. splines compared with keys have many advantages

entries.label: mott6-c-0042
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0042 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that because usually four or more splines are used, as compared with one or two keys, a more uniform transfer of torque and a lower loading on a given part of the shaft/hub interface result. spline with four or more teeth produces more uniform torque transfer and lower loading on a given part of the shaft/hub interface than one or two keys

entries.label: mott6-c-0043
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0043 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that splines are integral with the shaft, so that no relative motion can occur of the kind that can occur between a key and the shaft, and that splines are accurately machined to provide a controlled fit between mating internal and external splines. splines are integral with the shaft, so no relative motion can occur as between a key and the shaft

entries.label: mott6-c-0044
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0044 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that sliding motion between a standard parallel key and the mating element should not be permitted, whereas a spline surface is often hardened to resist wear and to facilitate use in applications where axial motion of the mating element is desired. sliding motion between a standard parallel key and the mating element should not be permitted

entries.label: mott6-c-0045
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0045 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that because of the multiple splines on the shaft, the mating element can be indexed to various positions. multiple splines on a shaft allow the mating element to be indexed to various angular positions

entries.label: mott6-c-0046
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0046 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that the involute spline form is preferred because it provides self-centering of the mating element and because it can be machined with standard hobs used to cut gear teeth. involute spline form is preferred over the straight-sided form, because it self-centres the mating element and can be cut with standard gear hobs

entries.label: mott6-c-0047
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0047 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that the torque capacity for sae straight-sided splines is based on a limit of 1000 psi bearing stress on the sides of the splines, from which t = 1000 n r h is derived, where n is the number of splines, r the mean radius and h the spline depth. the torque capacity is per inch of spline length. torque capacity of sae straight-sided splines is based on a limit of 1000 psi bearing stress on the sides of the splines, giving t = 1000 n r h per inch of spline length

entries.label: mott6-c-0048
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0048 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that the sae spline permanent fit a is used when the mating part is not to be moved after installation, fit b when the mating part will be moved along the shaft without a torque load, and fit c when the mating part must be moved under load; the spline depth h and minor diameter d differ between the fits. sae spline fit classes a, b and c correspond to permanent installation, movement along the shaft without torque load, and movement under load

entries.label: mott6-c-0049
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0049 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution in its design procedure for parallel keys, mott states that if the computed minimum key length is longer than the hub length, a higher-strength material must be selected and the design repeated, or alternatively two keys or a spline can be used instead of a single key. a spline or two keys may be used instead of a single key, when the computed key length exceeds the hub length

entries.label: mott6-c-0050
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0050 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott introduces methods of attaching power-transmitting elements to shafts without keys or splines, noting that in most cases these designs have not been standardised and that analysis of individual cases considering the forces and manner of loading is necessary. attachment of power-transmitting elements without keys or splines is possible by pinning, keyless friction connections and similar methods, mostly not standardised

entries.label: mott6-c-0051
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — verification
entries.text: mott6-c-0051 machine elements in mechanical design — verification mott states that if a satisfactory analysis of a keyless attachment method is not possible, testing of the assembly is recommended. keyless attachment design requires testing of the assembly when a satisfactory analysis is not possible

entries.label: mott6-c-0052
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0052 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that the diameter of a pin is sometimes purposely made small to ensure that the pin will break if a moderate overload is encountered, in order to protect critical parts of a mechanism, and that such a pin is called a shear pin. shear pin is a pin deliberately undersized so that it breaks on a moderate overload, protecting critical parts

entries.label: mott6-c-0053
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — shaft-hub-connection
entries.text: mott6-c-0053 machine elements in mechanical design — shaft-hub-connection mott states that the presence of any of the pin-type connections produces stress concentrations in the shaft. pin-type connections produce stress concentrations in the shaft

entries.label: mott6-c-0054
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — substitution
entries.text: mott6-c-0054 machine elements in mechanical design — substitution mott states that using a steel ring compressed tightly around a smooth shaft allows torque to be transmitted between the hub of a power-transmitting element and the shaft without a key, and describes a commercially available locking assembly employing opposed tapered rings drawn together by fasteners. a steel ring compressed around a smooth shaft allows torque transmission between hub and shaft without a key

entries.label: mott6-c-0060
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — verification
entries.text: mott6-c-0060 machine elements in mechanical design — verification mott states that there are two basic modes of potential failure for keys transmitting power: shear across the shaft/hub interface, and compression failure due to the bearing action between the sides of the key and the shaft or hub material. keys transmitting power have two basic potential failure modes: shear across the shaft/hub interface and bearing compression on the key sides

entries.label: mott6-c-0061
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — verification
entries.text: mott6-c-0061 machine elements in mechanical design — verification mott sets the shearing stress equal to a design stress in shear based on the maximum shear stress theory of failure, tau_d = 0.5 s_y / n, and obtains the minimum required key length for shear as l_min = 2t / (tau_d d w), where t is torque, d the shaft diameter and w the key width. minimum key length for shear is computed from l_min = 2t / (tau_d d w), with tau_d = 0.5 s_y / n from the maximum shear stress theory

entries.label: mott6-c-0062
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — verification
entries.text: mott6-c-0062 machine elements in mechanical design — verification mott states that failure in bearing relates to the compressive stress on the side of the key, the shaft keyseat or the hub keyseat; the compression area is the same for each, so failure occurs on the surface with the lowest compressive yield strength. bearing failure of a key connection occurs on whichever of key, shaft keyseat or hub keyseat has the lowest compressive yield strength

entries.label: mott6-c-0063
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — verification
entries.text: mott6-c-0063 machine elements in mechanical design — verification in its design procedure for parallel keys, mott states that in typical industrial applications a design factor n = 3 is adequate to accommodate accidental overloads and shock. design factor for parallel keys in typical industrial applications is recommended as n = 3, to accommodate accidental overloads and shock

entries.label: mott6-c-0064
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — verification
entries.text: mott6-c-0064 machine elements in mechanical design — verification mott states that where a rectangular key is used, or where the shaft or hub has lower strength than the key, the minimum lengths for bearing and for shear must both be computed and the larger governs; the result must be checked against the available hub length. required key length is governed by the larger of the lengths computed for shear and for bearing

entries.label: mott6-c-0070
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — bearing-life
entries.text: mott6-c-0070 machine elements in mechanical design — bearing-life mott states the relationship between load p and life l for rolling contact bearings as l2 / l1 = (p1 / p2)^k. relationship between rolling-bearing load and life is l2 / l1 = (p1 / p2)^k

entries.label: mott6-c-0071
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — bearing-life
entries.text: mott6-c-0071 machine elements in mechanical design — bearing-life mott gives the load/life exponent k as 3.00 for ball bearings and 3.33 for roller bearings. load/life exponent k takes the values 3.00 for ball bearings and 3.33 for roller bearings

entries.label: mott6-c-0072
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — bearing-life
entries.text: mott6-c-0072 machine elements in mechanical design — bearing-life mott states that the basic static load rating c_o is the load the bearing can withstand without permanent deformation of any component; exceeding it most probably indents a race, a failure referred to as brinelling, after which operation would be noisy and progressive failure would follow. basic static load rating c_o is the load a bearing can withstand without permanent deformation of any component

entries.label: mott6-c-0073
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — bearing-life
entries.text: mott6-c-0073 machine elements in mechanical design — bearing-life mott states that despite the use of very high strength steels, all rolling contact bearings have a finite life and will eventually fail due to fatigue because of the high contact stresses, the lighter the load the longer the life. rolling contact bearings have a finite life, eventually failing by fatigue due to high contact stresses

entries.label: mott6-c-0074
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — bearing-life
entries.text: mott6-c-0074 machine elements in mechanical design — bearing-life mott states that where manufacturer load data are reported for one million revolutions, the design life is l_d = (c / p_d)^k times 10^6 and the required basic dynamic load rating is c = p_d (l_d / 10^6)^(1/k), with design revolutions obtained from hours of operation and shaft speed. required basic dynamic load rating is computed from c = p_d (l_d / 10^6)^(1/k) for catalogue data rated at one million revolutions

entries.label: mott6-c-0075
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — bearing-life
entries.text: mott6-c-0075 machine elements in mechanical design — bearing-life mott states that the design life is specified by the designer considering the application, and provides a table of recommended design life in hours by application class as a guide. bearing design life is specified by the designer, considering the application, guided by a table of recommended values by application class

entries.label: mott6-c-0076
entries.sub: Machine Elements in Mechanical Design — bearing-life
entries.text: mott6-c-0076 machine elements in mechanical design — bearing-life mott states that the tabulated bearing data in the book are similar to those in manufacturers' catalogues, and that it is essential that published data from specific manufacturers be used in any real application. bearing selection for a real application requires published data from the specific manufacturer

entries.label: shigley10-c-0001
entries.text: shigley10-c-0001 shigley's mechanical engineering design — design-factor shigley defines the design factor n_d as the ratio of the loss-of-function strength to the allowable stress, and calls the deterministic form of this approach the classical method of design. design factor n_d is defined as loss-of-function strength divided by allowable stress

entries.label: shigley10-c-0002
entries.text: shigley10-c-0002 shigley's mechanical engineering design — design-factor shigley distinguishes the design factor n_d, chosen before the design is completed, from the factor of safety n, which is the value actually achieved after choices such as rounding up to a standard size. the two have the same definition but generally differ numerically. factor of safety n is distinguished from design factor n_d

entries.label: shigley10-c-0003
entries.text: shigley10-c-0003 shigley's mechanical engineering design — design-factor shigley states that all loss-of-function modes must be analyzed and that the mode leading to the smallest design factor governs. design factor evaluation requires analysis of all loss-of-function modes, with the smallest resulting factor governing

entries.label: shigley10-c-0004
entries.text: shigley10-c-0004 shigley's mechanical engineering design — design-factor shigley states that the stress and strength terms used in the design-factor equation must be of the same type and the same units, and must apply to the same critical location in the part. stress and strength terms in the design-factor equation must be of the same type and units, and applied at the same critical location

entries.label: shigley10-c-0005
entries.text: shigley10-c-0005 shigley's mechanical engineering design — design-factor shigley states that the designer must rely on experience, company policies and applicable codes to arrive at an appropriate design factor, because of the difficulty of evaluating the uncertainties involved. assignment of a design factor value requires experience, company policies and applicable codes

entries.label: shigley10-c-0020
entries.text: shigley10-c-0020 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that keys are used to enable the transmission of torque from the shaft to the shaft-supported element, while pins are used for axial positioning and for the transfer of torque or thrust or both. keys and pins serve distinct roles: keys transmit torque, pins locate axially and transfer torque or thrust or both

entries.label: shigley10-c-0021
entries.text: shigley10-c-0021 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that pins are useful when the principal loading is shear and when both torsion and thrust are present. pins are useful when the principal loading is shear and both torsion and thrust are present

entries.label: shigley10-c-0022
entries.text: shigley10-c-0022 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that the maximum length of a key is limited by the hub length of the attached element and should generally not exceed about 1.5 times the shaft diameter, to avoid excessive twisting with the angular deflection of the shaft. maximum key length should not exceed about 1.5 times the shaft diameter

entries.label: shigley10-c-0023
entries.text: shigley10-c-0023 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that multiple keys may be used as necessary to carry greater loads, typically oriented at 90 degrees from one another. multiple keys may be used to carry greater loads, typically oriented at 90 degrees from one another

entries.label: shigley10-c-0024
entries.text: shigley10-c-0024 shigley's mechanical engineering design — design-factor shigley states that excessive safety factors should be avoided in key design, since in an overload situation it is desirable for the key to fail rather than more costly components. safety factor in key design should not be excessive, because it is desirable for the key to fail rather than costlier components

entries.label: shigley10-c-0025
entries.text: shigley10-c-0025 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that a setscrew is sometimes used along with a key to hold the hub axially and to minimise rotational backlash when the shaft rotates in both directions. setscrew used together with a key serves to hold the hub axially and minimise rotational backlash under bidirectional rotation

entries.label: shigley10-c-0026
entries.text: shigley10-c-0026 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that the woodruff key yields better concentricity after assembly of wheel and shaft, especially important at high speeds, that it is useful when a wheel is positioned against a shoulder because the keyslot need not be machined into the shoulder stress-concentration region, and that its deeper penetration helps prevent key rolling in smaller shafts. woodruff key yields better concentricity after assembly, which is especially important at high speeds

entries.label: shigley10-c-0027
entries.text: shigley10-c-0027 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that a sled-runner keyseat reduces the stress concentration at the end of the keyseat by eliminating the abrupt end, but can only be used when definite longitudinal key positioning is not necessary, and is not as suitable near a shoulder. sled-runner keyseat may be used only when definite longitudinal key positioning is not necessary

entries.label: shigley10-c-0028
entries.text: shigley10-c-0028 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that, unlike bolts and cap screws which depend on tension to develop a clamping force, the setscrew depends on compression; its holding power comes from frictional resistance between collar and shaft together with any slight penetration of the setscrew into the shaft. setscrew develops clamping force by compression, unlike bolts and cap screws which depend on tension

entries.label: shigley10-c-0029
entries.text: shigley10-c-0029 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that typical factors of safety applied to tabulated setscrew holding power are 1.5 to 2.0 for static loads and 4 to 8 for various dynamic loads, the tabulated values applying to both axial and tangential holding power. setscrew holding power is typically applied with factors of safety of 1.5 to 2.0 for static loads and 4 to 8 for various dynamic loads

entries.label: shigley10-c-0030
entries.text: shigley10-c-0030 shigley's mechanical engineering design — shaft-hub-connection shigley states that setscrews should have a length of about half of the shaft diameter, and notes that this also gives a rough rule for the radial thickness of a hub or collar. setscrew length should be about half the shaft diameter

entries.label: shigley10-c-0040
entries.text: shigley10-c-0040 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley describes splines as essentially stubby gear teeth formed on the outside of the shaft and on the inside of the hub of the load-transmitting component, and notes that sae and ansi publish standards for splines. splines are essentially stubby gear teeth formed on the shaft outside diameter and the hub bore

entries.label: shigley10-c-0041
entries.text: shigley10-c-0041 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that splines are generally much more expensive to manufacture than keys and are usually not necessary for simple torque transmission. splines compared with keys are generally much more expensive to manufacture, and usually unnecessary for simple torque transmission

entries.label: shigley10-c-0042
entries.text: shigley10-c-0042 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that splines are typically used to transfer high torques. splines are typically used to transfer high torques

entries.label: shigley10-c-0043
entries.text: shigley10-c-0043 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that one feature of a spline is that it can be made with a reasonably loose slip fit to allow large axial motion between shaft and component while still transmitting torque, which is useful for connecting shafts where relative motion is common, such as a tractor power take-off. spline with a reasonably loose slip fit allows large axial motion between shaft and component while still transmitting torque

entries.label: shigley10-c-0044
entries.text: shigley10-c-0044 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that stress-concentration factors for splines are greatest where the spline ends and blends into the shaft, but are generally quite moderate. spline stress-concentration factors are greatest at the point where the spline ends and blends into the shaft, but are generally quite moderate

entries.label: shigley10-c-0045
entries.text: shigley10-c-0045 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that for cases of low torque transmission various means of transmitting torque are available, including pins, setscrews in hubs, tapered fits and press fits. low torque transmission may be achieved by pins, setscrews in hubs, tapered fits and press fits

entries.label: shigley10-c-0046
entries.text: shigley10-c-0046 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that press and shrink fits for securing hubs to shafts are used both for torque transfer and for preserving axial location, and that the resulting stress-concentration factor is usually quite small. press and shrink fits are used for both torque transfer and axial location, with a usually quite small stress-concentration factor

entries.label: shigley10-c-0047
entries.text: shigley10-c-0047 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that a split hub clamped to the shaft with screws allows for disassembly and lateral adjustments. split hub clamped with screws allows disassembly and lateral adjustments

entries.label: shigley10-c-0048
entries.text: shigley10-c-0048 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that tapered fits, often used on the overhanging end of a shaft with a nut on a threaded shaft end, are useful because they can be disassembled, but do not provide good axial location of the wheel on the shaft. tapered fit between shaft and mounted device permits disassembly but does not provide good axial location of the mounted element

entries.label: shigley10-c-0049
entries.text: shigley10-c-0049 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that interference fits between a shaft and its components can sometimes be used effectively to minimise the need for shoulders and keyways. interference fits can minimise the need for shoulders and keyways

entries.label: shigley10-c-0050
entries.text: shigley10-c-0050 shigley's mechanical engineering design — substitution shigley states that the torque an interference fit can transmit is estimated by a simple friction analysis at the interface, the friction force being the product of the coefficient of friction and the normal force, giving a torque capacity t = (pi/2) f p l d^2, where f is the coefficient of friction, p the interface pressure, l the hub length and d the nominal shaft diameter. torque capacity of an interference fit is estimated by a friction analysis giving t = (pi/2) f p l d^2

entries.label: shigley10-c-0051
entries.text: shigley10-c-0051 shigley's mechanical engineering design — verification shigley states that the minimum interference should be used to determine the minimum pressure, which in turn bounds the maximum torque the joint should be designed to transmit without slipping; the maximum interference is used instead to check for excessive stress. interference-fit torque capacity check must use the minimum interference, to obtain the minimum pressure and hence the maximum torque the joint may be designed to transmit without slipping

entries.label: shigley10-c-0052
entries.text: shigley10-c-0052 shigley's mechanical engineering design — verification shigley states that a press fit produces a stress-concentration effect in the shaft bending stress near the ends of the hub, due to the sudden change from compressed to uncompressed material, that hub geometry makes generalised values difficult to report, and that for first estimates values are typically not greater than 2. stress concentration due to a press fit occurs in the shaft bending stress near the ends of the hub; first estimates are typically not greater than 2

entries.label: shigley10-c-0060
entries.text: shigley10-c-0060 shigley's mechanical engineering design — verification shigley states that failure of a key can be by direct shear or by bearing stress, that the shaft diameter determines standard sizes for key width, height and depth, and that the designer chooses the key length to carry the torsional load. key failure may occur by direct shear or by bearing stress

entries.label: shigley10-c-0061
entries.text: shigley10-c-0061 shigley's mechanical engineering design — verification shigley states that it is necessary to know where shaft discontinuities such as keyways, holes and splines will be, in order to determine the critical locations for analysis. location of shaft discontinuities must be known to determine the critical locations for stress analysis

entries.label: shigley10-c-0062
entries.text: shigley10-c-0062 shigley's mechanical engineering design — verification shigley cites published stress-concentration charts giving factors for an end-milled keyseat as a function of the ratio of the groove-bottom radius to the shaft diameter, with separate values for bending and for torsion, and with a further distinction for torsion with the key in place. stress-concentration factors for an end-milled keyseat are cited from published stress-concentration charts, as a function of the groove radius to shaft diameter ratio

entries.label: shigley10-c-0070
entries.text: shigley10-c-0070 shigley's mechanical engineering design — bearing-life shigley states that the rating life, a term sanctioned by the abma and used by most manufacturers, is the number of revolutions or hours at constant speed that 90 percent of a group of nominally identical bearings will achieve or exceed before the failure criterion develops; it is the 10th percentile of the revolutions-to-failure distribution. rating life is defined as the number of revolutions, or hours at constant speed, that 90 percent of a group of nominally identical bearings will achieve or exceed before the failure criterion develops

entries.label: shigley10-c-0071
entries.text: shigley10-c-0071 shigley's mechanical engineering design — bearing-life shigley states that the terms minimum life, l10 life and b10 life are used as synonyms for rating life. minimum life, l10 life and b10 life are synonyms for rating life

entries.label: shigley10-c-0072

entries.label: align-c-0001
entries.text: align-c-0001 agrees failure modes of a key transmitting torque both books state that a key can fail by direct shear or by bearing (compressive) stress, and both treat the two as checks to be made together. no difference in scope or condition. mott states that there are two basic modes of potential failure for keys transmitting power: shear across the shaft/hub interface, and compression failure due to the bearing action between the sides of the key and the shaft or hub material. shigley states that failure of a key can be by direct shear or by bearing stress, that the shaft diameter determines standard sizes for key width, height and depth, and that the designer chooses the key length to carry the torsional load.

entries.label: align-c-0004
entries.text: align-c-0004 refines catalogue rating-life basis practically important. applying mott's c = p_d (l_d/10^6)^(1/k) to a catalogue rated on a different basis gives a wrong answer. shigley's claim refines and bounds mott's assumption; both are kept. mott states that where manufacturer load data are reported for one million revolutions, the design life is l_d = (c / p_d)^k times 10^6 and the required basic dynamic load rating is c = p_d (l_d / 10^6)^(1/k), with design revolutions obtained from hours of operation and shaft speed. shigley states that each manufacturer chooses a specific rating life for which load ratings are reported, that the most commonly used rating life is 10^6 revolutions, and that at least one well-known manufacturer instead rates bearings at 3000 hours at 500 rev/min, equal to 90 million revolutions.

entries.label: align-c-0005
entries.text: align-c-0005 differsinscope splines compared with keys not a contradiction. the books foreground different evaluation criteria and different design situations. merging them into a single verdict on splines would destroy exactly the information a designer needs. both are retained and the substitution assessments cite both. mott states that the advantages of splines over keys are many. shigley states that splines are generally much more expensive to manufacture than keys and are usually not necessary for simple torque transmission.

entries.label: align-c-0006
entries.text: align-c-0006 differsinassumption how conservative a key design should be the two are not formally contradictory: mott gives a number, shigley gives a direction, and n = 3 is not necessarily 'excessive'. but they express opposite design intents -- survive the overload versus act as the fuse -- and which applies depends on whether the key is meant to be sacrificial. left explicitly unresolved. any rule derived from either must state which intent it assumes. in its design procedure for parallel keys, mott states that in typical industrial applications a design factor n = 3 is adequate to accommodate accidental overloads and shock. shigley states that excessive safety factors should be avoided in key design, since in an overload situation it is desirable for the key to fail rather than more costly components.

entries.label: align-c-0007
entries.text: align-c-0007 complements axial motion of a hub relative to the shaft while torque is transmitted mott states that sliding motion between a standard parallel key and the mating element should not be permitted; shigley states that a spline with a loose slip fit allows large axial motion while still transmitting torque. together they establish, from two independent sources, the condition under which a key cannot be used and a spline can. this pair is the evidential basis of substitution assessment sa-001. mott states that sliding motion between a standard parallel key and the mating element should not be permitted, whereas a spline surface is often hardened to resist wear and to facilitate use in applications where axial motion of the mating element is desired. shigley states that one feature of a spline is that it can be made with a reasonably loose slip fit to allow large axial motion between shaft and component while still transmitting torque, which is useful for connecting shafts where relative motion is common, such as a tractor power take-off.

entries.label: align-c-0008
entries.text: align-c-0008 complements using more than one key to carry a larger load mott offers two keys or a spline as the remedy when a single key would be longer than the hub. shigley states that multiple keys may be used to carry greater loads and adds the practical detail that they are typically oriented at 90 degrees apart. shigley supplies the arrangement mott omits. in its design procedure for parallel keys, mott states that if the computed minimum key length is longer than the hub length, a higher-strength material must be selected and the design repeated, or alternatively two keys or a spline can be used instead of a single key. shigley states that multiple keys may be used as necessary to carry greater loads, typically oriented at 90 degrees from one another.

entries.label: align-c-0009
entries.text: align-c-0009 agrees definition of the design factor both define the design factor as the ratio of a strength to an allowable stress, and both derive a design stress by dividing strength by the factor. mott defines the design factor n as a measure of the relative safety of a load-carrying component. in most cases the strength of the material is divided by n to obtain a design stress (also called the allowable stress), and the actual stress must be less than the design stress. shigley defines the design factor n_d as the ratio of the loss-of-function strength to the allowable stress, and calls the deterministic form of this approach the classical method of design.

entries.label: align-c-0010
entries.text: align-c-0010 differsinterminology naming of the safety margin before and after design a reader combining formulas from both books must check which of the two roles each symbol plays; they are not blindly interchangeable. mott defines the design factor n as a measure of the relative safety of a load-carrying component. in most cases the strength of the material is divided by n to obtain a design stress (also called the allowable stress), and the actual stress must be less than the design stress. shigley distinguishes the design factor n_d, chosen before the design is completed, from the factor of safety n, which is the value actually achieved after choices such as rounding up to a standard size. the two have the same definition but generally differ numerically.

entries.label: align-c-0011
entries.text: align-c-0011 complements when to choose a woodruff key non-overlapping rationales for the same element. taken together they give a fuller applicability profile than either book alone. mott states that where light loading and relatively easy assembly and disassembly are desired, the woodruff key should be considered. shigley states that the woodruff key yields better concentricity after assembly of wheel and shaft, especially important at high speeds, that it is useful when a wheel is positioned against a shoulder because the keyslot need not be machined into the shoulder stress-concentration region, and that its deeper penetration helps prevent key rolling in smaller shafts.

entries.label: align-c-0012
entries.text: align-c-0012 complements stress concentration introduced by a shaft/hub connection mott states that pin-type connections produce stress concentrations in the shaft; shigley states that the stress-concentration factor from a press or shrink fit is usually quite small. read together they support a comparative ranking, which neither book states outright. any such ranking is an analyst inference and is marked as one. mott states that the presence of any of the pin-type connections produces stress concentrations in the shaft. shigley states that press and shrink fits for securing hubs to shafts are used both for torque transfer and for preserving axial location, and that the resulting stress-concentration factor is usually quite small.

entries.label: align-c-0013
entries.text: align-c-0013 agrees necessity of using the specific manufacturer's published data both books direct the designer to manufacturer data for any real bearing selection, and both present their own tabulated values as illustrative. mott states that the tabulated bearing data in the book are similar to those in manufacturers' catalogues, and that it is essential that published data from specific manufacturers be used in any real application. shigley states that each manufacturer chooses a specific rating life for which load ratings are reported, that the most commonly used rating life is 10^6 revolutions, and that at least one well-known manufacturer instead rates bearings at 3000 hours at 500 rev/min, equal to 90 million revolutions.

entries.label: align-c-0014
entries.text: align-c-0014 differsinscope torque capacity of a spline connection complementary in practice but not comparable as statements: one is quantitative and narrow, the other qualitative and broad. only mott's claim can support a capacity calculation, and only within its stated unit system. mott states that the torque capacity for sae straight-sided splines is based on a limit of 1000 psi bearing stress on the sides of the splines, from which t = 1000 n r h is derived, where n is the number of splines, r the mean radius and h the spline depth. the torque capacity is per inch of spline length. shigley states that splines are typically used to transfer high torques.

entries.label: align-c-0015
entries.text: align-c-0015 complements why rolling bearings have a finite life mott gives the physical reason (fatigue under high contact stress); shigley gives the statistical definition of the life that is quoted (the 10th percentile of the failure distribution). neither is complete alone. mott states that despite the use of very high strength steels, all rolling contact bearings have a finite life and will eventually fail due to fatigue because of the high contact stresses, the lighter the load the longer the life. shigley states that the rating life, a term sanctioned by the abma and used by most manufacturers, is the number of revolutions or hours at constant speed that 90 percent of a group of nominally identical bearings will achieve or exceed before the failure criterion develops; it is the 10th percentile of the revolutions-to-failure distribution.

entries.label: Reversing Loading

entries.label: Book
entries.text: book 도서 ev:book a work, independent of any particular edition or printing.

entries.label: Book Edition
entries.text: book edition 판 ev:bookedition a specific edition of a book. claims are attached to editions, never to works, because pagination, equation numbering and content differ between editions.

entries.label: Candidate Design Rule
entries.text: candidate design rule ev:candidatedesignrule a normalized claim proposed for promotion into the rule layer, not yet accepted.

entries.label: Chapter
entries.text: chapter 장 ev:chapter

entries.label: Claim
entries.text: claim 주장 ev:claim a single assertion attributed to a source, held as data rather than as an ontology axiom, so that it can be conditioned, contradicted, revised or rejected without touching the schema. claims are abox individuals. promotion of a claim into a tbox axiom or an executable rule is a separate, human-authorised step.

entries.label: Claim Alignment
entries.text: claim alignment 주장 정렬 ev:claimalignment a reified comparison of two claims from different sources, recording how they relate without merging them. conflicting claims are preserved side by side. reconciliation is never silent.

entries.label: Concept Alignment
entries.text: concept alignment 개념 정렬 ev:conceptalignment a mapping between a source-specific term or symbol and a core-ontology concept, or between the corresponding terms of two sources.

entries.label: Design Procedure
entries.text: design procedure 설계 절차 ev:designprocedure an ordered procedure printed in a source, cited as a unit because its steps are only valid together.

entries.label: Equation
entries.text: equation 수식 ev:equation

entries.label: Evidence
entries.text: evidence 근거 ev:evidence anything that supports or contradicts a claim.

entries.label: Evidence Span
entries.text: evidence span 근거 구간 ev:evidencespan a located, quotable region of a source document: a document, a page, a block, optionally a bounding box, and the text that was actually extracted from it. excerpts are kept short. the purpose of the stored text is to make the citation verifiable by re-reading the page, not to reproduce the book.

entries.label: Example Problem
entries.text: example problem 예제 ev:exampleproblem

entries.label: Extracted Claim
entries.text: extracted claim ev:extractedclaim a claim as first obtained from the source text, before normalisation.

entries.label: Figure
entries.text: figure 그림 ev:figure

entries.label: Manufacturer Catalog
entries.text: manufacturer catalog 제조사 카탈로그 ev:manufacturercatalog a manufacturer's published data source, cited but not reproduced.

entries.label: Normalized Claim
entries.text: normalized claim ev:normalizedclaim a claim restated in controlled vocabulary, with conditions and units made explicit.

entries.label: Page
entries.text: page 페이지 ev:page one page of one source document, carrying both its zero-based pdf index and its printed label.

entries.label: Section
entries.text: section 절 ev:section

entries.label: Source Document
entries.text: source document ev:sourcedocument the concrete file that was processed, identified by file name and sha-256, so that provenance cannot silently drift onto a different scan of the same edition.

entries.label: Standard
entries.text: standard 표준 ev:standard a published standard referenced by a source. referencing a standard is not the same as reproducing it: the ontology records that a standard governs a value, not the value itself, unless the source printed it.

entries.label: Table
entries.text: table 표 ev:table

entries.label: Terminology Alignment
entries.text: terminology alignment ev:terminologyalignment a concept alignment concerned specifically with vocabulary or symbol usage.

entries.label: Variable
entries.text: variable 변수 ev:variable a symbol appearing in an equation, together with its meaning, dimension and preferred unit, scoped to the source that used it. variables are source-scoped on purpose. mott's k and shigley's a are the same physical exponent but are not merged; they are linked through a conceptalignment instead.

entries.label: //www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#Concept
entries.text: //www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#concept http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#concept declared outside the core modules; shown so that its subclasses are not stranded.

entries.label: Acceptance Criterion
entries.text: acceptance criterion 합격 기준 mdcore:acceptancecriterion the condition a verification result must meet for the design to be judged acceptable.

entries.label: Alternative Evaluation
entries.text: alternative evaluation 대안 평가 mdcore:alternativeevaluation a reified statement that a design alternative attains a stated level on a stated criterion, in a stated context, on stated authority. reified because the same alternative scores differently on the same criterion in different contexts, and because the provenance of each score must travel with it.

entries.label: Analytical Model
entries.text: analytical model mdcore:analyticalmodel a derived model of behaviour, stated with its assumptions and validity conditions.

entries.label: Assembly
entries.text: assembly 조립체 mdcore:assembly a designed artifact produced by joining two or more artifacts through interfaces, and which is handled as a single item at the next level of assembly.

entries.label: Assembly Condition
entries.text: assembly condition 조립 조건 mdcore:assemblycondition

entries.label: Availability Constraint
entries.text: availability constraint mdcore:availabilityconstraint constraint arising from procurement lead time or from whether an element is a standard, catalogue item.

entries.label: Behavior
entries.text: behavior 거동 mdcore:behavior a physical process by which a structure produces a function under given operating conditions, described in terms of the quantities that are exchanged or transformed. behavior answers 'by what mechanism?'. 'transmit torque' is a function; 'transfer load by shear across a shaft/hub interface' is a behavior.

entries.label: Calculation Method
entries.text: calculation method 계산 방법 mdcore:calculationmethod

entries.label: Candidate Set
entries.text: candidate set mdcore:candidateset the set of design alternatives admitted to comparison for a given design problem, together with the filter that produced it. reified so that the reason an alternative was excluded from consideration is recoverable, not lost.

entries.label: Combined Loading
entries.text: combined loading mdcore:combinedloading two or more load types acting together, e.g. bending with torsion.

entries.label: Component
entries.text: component 구성 부품 mdcore:component a designed artifact treated as atomic at the level of decomposition currently under consideration. atomicity is relative to the analysis, not absolute: a rolling bearing is a component to a shaft designer and an assembly to a bearing manufacturer.

entries.label: Constraint
entries.text: constraint 제약조건 mdcore:constraint a requirement that bounds the admissible solution space rather than expressing a desired level of performance; it is satisfied or violated, and is not traded off. distinguishing constraint from the general requirement matters for decision-making: constraints filter the candidate set before any weighting or scoring is applied.

entries.label: Contaminated Environment
entries.text: contaminated environment mdcore:contaminatedenvironment

entries.label: Corrosive Environment
entries.text: corrosive environment 부식 환경 mdcore:corrosiveenvironment

entries.label: Cyclic Loading
entries.text: cyclic loading 반복하중 mdcore:cyclicloading load that varies repeatedly with time, so that fatigue is a candidate failure mechanism.

entries.label: Decision Rationale
entries.text: decision rationale 결정 근거 mdcore:decisionrationale the stated reasoning for a design decision, including the criteria that dominated and the alternatives rejected.

entries.label: Design Alternative
entries.text: design alternative 설계 대안 mdcore:designalternative a candidate solution concept that could be adopted to satisfy a design problem: a class of artifact, a working principle, or a specific configuration. a designalternative is a *solution concept*, not an individual manufactured item. 'parallel key connection' is an alternative; 'the key in gearbox serial 4471' is not.

entries.label: Design Decision
entries.text: design decision 설계 결정 mdcore:designdecision a recorded commitment to one alternative for a design problem, with the evaluations and rationale that supported it.

entries.label: Design Feature
entries.text: design feature 설계 특징 mdcore:designfeature any deliberate characteristic of an artifact -- geometric, material, dimensional or procedural -- introduced to influence behaviour, for example to mitigate a failure mode. broader than geometryfeature: a surface treatment or a specified fit is a designfeature but not a geometryfeature.

entries.label: Design Modification
entries.text: design modification 설계 변경 mdcore:designmodification a change to geometry, material, tolerance, interface or process that must be carried out before a candidate can take the baseline's place.

entries.label: Design Problem
entries.text: design problem 설계 문제 mdcore:designproblem a stated need for a design solution, characterised by the functions required, the operating context, and the requirements and constraints that a solution must satisfy.

entries.label: Design Rule
entries.text: design rule 설계 규칙 mdcore:designrule a conditional statement of the form 'in context c, for requirement set r, do or prefer x', held as a citable object with its own provenance and review state. every designrule must either name an applicable context or declare mdcore:contextunspecified true. a rule with neither is invalid.

entries.label: Designed Artifact
entries.text: designed artifact 설계 대상물 mdcore:designedartifact any human-made entity that is the intended outcome of a design process, and about which functions, requirements and design decisions can be asserted. deliberately domain-neutral: a designed artifact may be mechanical, electrical, software or organisational. use for the thing being designed, not for the design description of it. a drawing of a shaft is a document, not a designedartifact.

entries.label: Dimensional Inspection
entries.text: dimensional inspection mdcore:dimensionalinspection

entries.label: Economic Condition
entries.text: economic condition 경제적 조건 mdcore:economiccondition

entries.label: Engineering Calculation
entries.text: engineering calculation mdcore:engineeringcalculation a closed-form design calculation, typically a sizing or stress check.

entries.label: Environmental Condition
entries.text: environmental condition 환경 조건 mdcore:environmentalcondition

entries.label: Evaluation Criterion
entries.text: evaluation criterion 평가 기준 mdcore:evaluationcriterion a dimension along which design alternatives are compared, derived from a requirement or from a stakeholder concern.

entries.label: External Authority Kind
entries.text: external authority kind mdcore:externalauthoritykind the kind of external source that must supply what the textbooks left unspecified.

entries.label: Failure Consequence
entries.text: failure consequence mdcore:failureconsequence the effect of a failure mode on the containing system, including whether the failure is benign, protective, or damaging to adjacent components. needed to represent deliberately sacrificial elements, where failure of one part is the intended way to protect others.

entries.label: Failure Mechanism
entries.text: failure mechanism 고장 메커니즘 mdcore:failuremechanism the physical, chemical or tribological process by which a failure mode develops: fatigue crack growth, plastic yielding, adhesive wear, corrosion, creep, fretting.

entries.label: Failure Mode
entries.text: failure mode 고장 모드 mdcore:failuremode the manner in which an artifact ceases to perform a required function, described observably: fracture, excessive deflection, loss of clamping, surface pitting, loosening.

entries.label: Fatigue Test
entries.text: fatigue test mdcore:fatiguetest

entries.label: Frequent Assembly
entries.text: frequent assembly mdcore:frequentassembly

entries.label: Frequent Disassembly
entries.text: frequent disassembly mdcore:frequentdisassembly

entries.label: Function
entries.text: function 기능 mdcore:function an intended, solution-neutral effect that a designed artifact is required to produce, expressed as a transformation of energy, material, motion, force or information. name functions as verb phrases ('transmit torque from shaft to hub'), never as element names ('key'). a function that can only be stated by naming one solution is not solution-neutral and is probably a requirement or a designalternative in disguise.

entries.label: Function Decomposition
entries.text: function decomposition 기능 분해 mdcore:functiondecomposition a reified statement that one function is fulfilled by a named set of sub-functions under a stated rationale. reified so that competing decompositions of the same function can coexist and be compared, rather than being merged.

entries.label: Functional Test
entries.text: functional test mdcore:functionaltest

entries.label: Geometry Feature
entries.text: geometry feature 형상 특징 mdcore:geometryfeature a named, bounded portion of an artifact's shape that carries design intent, for example a groove, a fillet, a shoulder or a hole. geometry features are the usual carriers of stress concentration and of manufacturing and inspection requirements.

entries.label: Inspection Method
entries.text: inspection method 검사 방법 mdcore:inspectionmethod

entries.label: Interface
entries.text: interface 인터페이스 mdcore:interface a region, surface or logical boundary at which two artifacts meet and exchange force, motion, energy, matter or information. interfaces carry the compatibility conditions that decide whether one design alternative can physically replace another. interface is reified rather than modelled as a bare relation because substitution reasoning must attach conditions, tolerances and required modifications to the junction itself.

entries.label: Interface Compatibility Level
entries.text: interface compatibility level mdcore:interfacecompatibilitylevel

entries.label: Kinematic Condition
entries.text: kinematic condition 운동 조건 mdcore:kinematiccondition the motion regime in which the artifact operates.

entries.label: Life Test
entries.text: life test mdcore:lifetest

entries.label: Lifecycle Condition
entries.text: lifecycle condition mdcore:lifecyclecondition a condition arising from how the artifact is made, assembled, serviced or retired.

entries.label: Linear Motion
entries.text: linear motion 직선운동 mdcore:linearmotion

entries.label: Loading Condition
entries.text: loading condition 하중 조건 mdcore:loadingcondition how force, moment or pressure is applied over time.

entries.label: Lubrication Condition
